t: may he show favor to/ us

x.ASV: For the Chief Musician; on stringed instruments. A Psalm, a Song. God be merciful unto us, and bless us, And cause his face to shine upon us; [Selah
x.Darby: To the chief Musician. On stringed instruments. A Psalm: a Song. God be gracious unto us, and bless us, [and] cause his face to shine upon us; Selah,
x.KJV: To the chief Musician on Neginoth, A Psalm or Song. God be merciful unto us, and bless us; and cause his face to shine upon us; Selah.
x.YLT: To the Overseer, with stringed instruments. --A Psalm, a Song. God doth favour us and bless us, Doth cause His face to shine with us. Selah.

nt: The psalmist is speaking of God showing his favor as if God’s **face** were a light that could **shine** on people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may he show us his favor]

x.ASV: That thy way may be known upon earth, Thy salvation among all nations.
x.Darby: That thy way may be known upon earth, thy salvation among all nations.
x.KJV: That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations.
x.YLT: For the knowledge in earth of Thy way, among all nations of Thy salvation.

nt: Here the word **for** marks **the knowing of your way** as the goal or purpose of the psalmist’s prayer for God’s blessing in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that people may know your way]

The psalmist is speaking of how God acts as if that were a **way** or path that God walks along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [how you act]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and for the knowing of your salvation among all of the nations]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how you save people]
The pronoun **your** refers to God in both instances. Alternate translation: [God’s way … God’s salvation among all the nations]

x.ASV: Let the peoples praise thee, O God; Let all the peoples praise thee.
x.Darby: Let the peoples praise thee, OGod, let all the peoples praise thee.
x.KJV: Let the people praise thee, O God; let all the people praise thee.
x.YLT: Praise Thee do peoples, O God, Praise Thee do peoples, all of them.

nt: יוֹד֖וּ⁠ךָ עַמִּ֥ים ׀ אֱלֹהִ֑ים י֝וֹד֗וּ⁠ךָ עַמִּ֥ים כֻּלָּֽ⁠ם

These two phrases **May the peoples thank you, God** and **may the peoples thank you, all of them** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with some different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [May all the peoples thank you, God] or [May all the peoples thank you, God; indeed, may everyone in the world thank you]

x.ASV: Oh let the nations be glad and sing for joy; For thou wilt judge the peoples with equity, And govern the nations upon earth. [Selah
x.Darby: Let the nations rejoice and sing for joy: for thou wilt judge the peoples equitably; and the nations upon earth, thou wilt guide them. Selah.
x.KJV: O let the nations be glad and sing for joy: for thou shalt judge the people righteously, and govern the nations upon earth. Selah.

nt: יִֽשְׂמְח֥וּ וִֽ⁠ירַנְּנ֗וּ לְאֻ֫מִּ֥ים כִּֽי־תִשְׁפֹּ֣ט עַמִּ֣ים מִישׁ֑וֹר וּ⁠לְאֻמִּ֓ים ׀ בָּ⁠אָ֖רֶץ תַּנְחֵ֣⁠ם סֶֽלָה

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because you judge the peoples {with} uprightness, and the nations on the earth, you guide them, may the nations rejoice and shout joyfully. Selah]
תִשְׁפֹּ֣ט עַמִּ֣ים מִישׁ֑וֹר וּ⁠לְאֻמִּ֓ים ׀ בָּ⁠אָ֖רֶץ תַּנְחֵ֣⁠ם

These two phrases **you judge the peoples with uprightness** and **the nations on the earth, you guide them** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [you judge and guide all the peoples on the earth with uprightness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **uprightness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [justly]

This verse is a refrain that repeats the exact words of [67:3](../067/003.md). If your language has a poetic way to indicate a refrain, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [May all the peoples thank you, God]

x.ASV: The earth hath yielded its increase: God, even our own God, will bless us.
x.Darby: The earth will yield her increase;God, ourGod, will bless us:
x.KJV: Then shall the earth yield her increase; and God, even our own God, shall bless us.
x.YLT: Earth hath given her increase, God doth bless us--our God,

nt: The psalmist is speaking of **the earth** as if it were a living thing that could **give** produce. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [There has been a good harvest from the earth]

The psalmist is not using the possessive form **our God** to indicate that the people of Israel possess or control God. Rather the psalmist is using these words to indicate that God is the one whom they worship. Alternate translation: [the God whom we worship]

x.ASV: God will bless us; And all the ends of the earth shall fear him.
x.Darby: God will bless us; and all the ends of the earth shall fear him.
x.KJV: God shall bless us; and all the ends of the earth shall fear him.
x.YLT: God doth bless us, and all ends of earth fear Him!

nt: Here, **all of the ends of the earth** represents people everywhere on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [people everywhere on the earth]
The pronoun **him** refers to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God]
